name: Pub/Sub
intent: Let a publisher announce an event to a topic, and let any number of independent subscribers each receive their own copy, without the publisher knowing who they are.
scenario: When an order is placed, the email service, the inventory service and the analytics service all need to react. New services will want to react too, later.
problem: If the order service calls each interested service directly, it must know about all of them, and every new consumer means changing and redeploying the order service. A slow or failing consumer also holds up the publisher. The producer ends up coupled to every consumer.

howItWorks.title: Publishers send to a topic, not to a recipient
howItWorks.text: The order service publishes an 'OrderPlaced' event to a topic. It has no idea who, if anyone, is listening, and it does not wait for them.

howItWorks.title: Each subscription gets its own copy (fan-out)
howItWorks.text: Every subscriber (or consumer group) receives every message, in its own queue and at its own speed. A slow analytics service never holds up email.

howItWorks.title: Consumer groups share work inside a subscription
howItWorks.text: Several instances of the same service can join one group. The message goes to one instance in the group, which spreads the load, while other groups still each get a full copy. This combines pub/sub with competing consumers.

howItWorks.title: Adding a subscriber needs no change to the publisher
howItWorks.text: A new fraud-check service simply subscribes. Some brokers (the servers that store and deliver messages) also retain history (log-based systems), so a new subscriber can replay old events, while others deliver only messages published after it joined.

howItWorks.title: Guarantees to design around
howItWorks.text: Delivery is usually at least once (a message can arrive twice), so subscribers must tolerate duplicates. Ordering is typically guaranteed only within a partition (a slice of the topic) or key, not across the whole topic. Events are facts about the past: name them that way (OrderPlaced), not as commands.

pros: Publisher and subscribers are decoupled: add or remove consumers freely
One event can drive many independent reactions
Slow or failing subscribers do not slow the publisher or each other
Works well for event-driven architectures and integrations
cons: Hard to see who reacts to an event, so flows are harder to trace and debug
No built-in reply: coordinating a result across subscribers needs extra design
Duplicates, reordering and lag must be handled by every subscriber
Schema changes to events can break unknown consumers
whenToUse: One event has several independent consumers, such as notifications, analytics and search indexing
You want to add consumers without touching the producer
You are building event-driven integrations between services
whenNotToUse: Exactly one consumer should handle each job (a queue is simpler)
The sender needs an immediate answer
There is only one consumer and it is unlikely to change
pitfalls: Publishing commands disguised as events, which brings hidden coupling back
Subscribers that are not idempotent (safe to run twice) and double-process redelivered events
Putting too much data in events, or too little, so consumers must call back
Changing an event's shape without versioning and breaking subscribers you do not know about

roles.label: Topic
roles.description: Copies each event to every subscription.

roles.label: Subscriber
roles.description: An independent service reacting to events.

quiz.question: An OrderPlaced topic has two subscriptions. The email service runs 3 instances in one consumer group, and the analytics service runs 1 instance in its own group. One OrderPlaced message is published. Who receives it?
options: All three email instances and the analytics instance
One of the three email instances and the analytics instance
One email instance only, and analytics gets it after email finishes
One instance chosen across all four, since there is one message
quiz.explanation: Each subscription (group) gets its own copy, and inside a group the message goes to a single instance. That is how fan-out combines with competing consumers.

quiz.question: An inventory subscriber decrements stock for every OrderPlaced event. After a broker timeout and redelivery, stock for one order dropped by 2. What is the best fix?
options: Acknowledge each message before processing so it is never delivered twice
Switch the broker to exactly-once delivery so duplicates cannot happen
Make the handler idempotent by recording processed event ids
Have the publisher wait until all subscribers confirm before it returns
quiz.explanation: Delivery is usually at least once, so duplicates are a normal case every subscriber must handle. Acknowledging first trades duplicates for lost messages. The publisher waiting on subscribers brings back the coupling pub/sub removes.

quiz.question: A checkout service publishes ChargeCard to a topic that only the payment service reads. It then waits for a ChargeResult message on another topic before it continues. Teams want to rename the message CardCharged to make it an event. Is that the right move?
options: No, it is a command with one consumer and a reply, so a direct call or queue fits
Yes, the new name turns the command into an event, so pub/sub is now the right fit
Yes, but add a consumer group to the payment service so it can scale across several instances
No, but add more subscribers so the topic is no longer one-to-one
quiz.explanation: Renaming does not change the fact that checkout depends on one specific consumer and a reply. Disguised commands bring hidden coupling back. Pub/sub fits when a fact is announced and any number of independent consumers may react.
